name: Play-action bootleg
seenIn: Covered in Football 101, Lesson 47: The backup-QB game plan: how offenses shrink the playbook (Luke Fahey, Drew Lock, Joe Fagnano)
what: The bootleg is a play-action pass where the quarterback fakes a handoff one way, then rolls out of the pocket the opposite way with the ball hidden on his hip. The defense flows toward the fake while the QB gets outside, away from the pass rush.

The receivers flood the side the QB is rolling to at three depths: one runs deep, one runs an out at about 12 yards, and a tight end or back sneaks into the flat just past the line. The QB reads one defender, usually the cornerback: if he sinks deep, throw the out; if he jumps the out, throw deep; if both are covered, dump it to the flat or run it.
Teams call it to slow down an aggressive run defense, to move the pocket when the line is struggling, and to make life simple for a young or backup QB, since he only has to read half the field.

caption: White: the dashed line is the running back's fake handoff to the left, the thick solid line is the QB rolling right (the bootleg), and the thin solid lines are the receivers' routes at three depths on the right side. Yellow dashes: linebackers stepping toward the fake.
spot: Usually from under center or a tight formation on early downs. The QB and RB mesh hard, the whole line and the defense lean one way, then the QB pops out the other side alone, often with no blocker in front of him, and looks to throw on the run to receivers stacked on that sideline.
beats: Run-hungry defenses whose linebackers and edge rushers chase the handoff and lose contain. Log it as Pass in the drill: it's a pass play built off a run fake, even if the QB ends up keeping it.
